title: Index calculus, end to end
one_liner: The whole algorithm run twice with every number shown: first in the multiplicative group of a prime field, then on an elliptic curve over F<sub>p<sup>2</sup></sub> using Semaev's summation polynomial.
index_meta: Worked example · F<sub>{{a_p}}</sub><sup>×</sup> and a curve over F<sub>{{b_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub>
description: Index calculus worked end to end: relation collection, linear algebra and descent in the multiplicative group of a prime field, then Gaudry's index calculus on an elliptic curve over F_p^2 with Semaev's summation polynomial, Weil restriction and a resultant.
standfirst: Index calculus is the attack that makes RSA and finite-field Diffie–Hellman keys large, and the attack that elliptic curves are chosen to escape. This note runs it end to end, twice, on groups small enough to show every relation.

facts.Part 1: Find x with {{a_g}}<sup>x</sup> ≡ {{a_h}} (mod {{a_p}}), using the primes up to {{a_bound}}
facts.Part 2: Find k with Q = kP on y<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>3</sup> + x + (1 + t) over F<sub>{{b_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub>, a group of {{b_n}} points
facts.Checked: Every logarithm on this page is verified by exponentiation or scalar multiplication each time the site is built
facts.What it shows: The mechanics. At these sizes neither part beats a generic attack, and Part 2 would not at any size; the last section says why

blocks.p: Choose a small set of group elements, the factor base. Find many random group elements whose logarithm you know and which can be written as products of factor-base elements; each one gives a linear equation in the unknown logarithms of the factor base. Solve those equations. Then write the target as a product of factor-base elements too, and its logarithm follows. The number field sieve is a far more elaborate version of the same plan.

The group is the nonzero integers modulo p = {{a_p}} under multiplication. This p is a safe prime: p − 1 = 2 · {{a_q}} with {{a_q}} prime, which will make the linear algebra simple. g = {{a_g}} generates the group. The target is h = {{a_h}}, and the task is to find x with {{a_g}}<sup>x</sup> ≡ {{a_h}} (mod {{a_p}}).
The factor base is the primes up to {{a_bound}}: {{a_base}}. An integer is {{a_bound}}-smooth if all its prime factors are in that list.

Pick a random exponent e, compute g<sup>e</sup> mod p as an ordinary integer between 1 and p − 1, and try to factor it over the factor base. If it factors as ∏ ℓ<sub>i</sub><sup>c<sub>i</sub></sup>, then taking logarithms gives one linear equation:

blocks.label: Logarithms to base g live modulo the group order, p − 1.

blocks.p: The search tried {{a_tried}} exponents and kept {{a_found}}, a rate of {{a_rate}}%. Exactly {{a_smooth_count}} of the {{a_pm1}} residues are {{a_bound}}-smooth, {{a_exact_rate}}%, so about {{a_expected_found}} hits were expected and this run found {{a_luck}}. The search stops as soon as its relations determine all {{a_base_size}} logarithms; here that took {{a_found}}.

The equations hold modulo {{a_pm1}} = 2 · {{a_q}}, which is not a prime, so they are solved in two pieces. Modulo {{a_q}} they are ordinary linear equations over a field, and Gaussian elimination gives each logarithm modulo {{a_q}}. Modulo 2 there is a shortcut: since g generates the group, log ℓ is even exactly when ℓ is a square modulo p, which the Legendre symbol decides. The Chinese remainder theorem then combines the two residues into the logarithm modulo {{a_pm1}}.
The target itself is not smooth, so multiply it by a random known power of g until the product is. After {{a_s_tries}} tries, s = {{a_s}} works:

blocks.label: So x + s is a sum of factor-base logarithms.

blocks.p: The factor-base bound B is a trade-off. A larger B makes random residues more likely to be smooth, but adds unknowns, so more relations and a bigger linear system are needed. Balancing the two, using the known density of smooth numbers, gives a running time of L<sub>p</sub>[1/2, c] for this basic method: slower than polynomial, much faster than the √p of a generic attack. The number field sieve reaches L<sub>p</sub>[1/3, 1.923] by making the numbers that must be smooth much smaller.

Everything above depends on one fact: an element of F<sub>p</sub><sup>×</sup> is also an integer, and integers factor. A point on an elliptic curve is not a product of anything. Part 2 is about what can be used instead.

Gaudry's idea is to use a subfield. Over F<sub>q<sup>n</sup></sub>, take the factor base to be the points whose x-coordinate lies in the subfield F<sub>q</sub>, and try to write a random point as a sum of n of them. The smallest case is n = 2. Here q = {{b_p}}, and F<sub>{{b_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub> is built as F<sub>{{b_p}}</sub>(t) with t<sup>2</sup> = {{b_r}}, so its elements are u + vt with u and v in F<sub>{{b_p}}</sub>.

The curve is y<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>3</sup> + x + (1 + t). Its group has {{b_n}} points. That number is prime, it lies in the Hasse interval [{{b_hasse_lo}}, {{b_hasse_hi}}], and the build finds a point of that order; since the interval is narrower than the order, the curve has exactly {{b_n}} points. P = {{b_P}}, and the target is Q = {{b_Q}}.

The factor base: for each x in F<sub>{{b_p}}</sub>, the curve has two points with that x-coordinate or none. {{b_classes}} of the {{b_p}} values give points, {{b_points}} points in all, about the half that one would expect. Since log(−P) = −log P, each pair ±P contributes one unknown. Write P<sub>x</sub> for the member of the pair with x-coordinate x that the code treats as positive.

Take R = mP for a random m, here m = {{b_a}}. Its x-coordinate is x<sub>R</sub> = {{b_xR}}. The question is whether R = ±P<sub>x<sub>1</sub></sub> ± P<sub>x<sub>2</sub></sub> for some x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub> in F<sub>{{b_p}}</sub>. Semaev's third summation polynomial answers exactly this: for the curve y<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>3</sup> + ax + b,

Now substitute x<sub>3</sub> = x<sub>R</sub> and the curve's a and b. Every coefficient is an element u + vt of F<sub>{{b_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub>, and the unknowns e<sub>1</sub>, e<sub>2</sub> are meant to lie in F<sub>{{b_p}}</sub>, so the equation holds only if the parts with and without t vanish separately. That splits one equation over F<sub>{{b_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub> into two over F<sub>{{b_p}}</sub>: this is the Weil restriction. For this R the two equations are

blocks.p: It has {{b_roots_phrase}}. From C<sub>1</sub>, e<sub>2</sub> = {{b_e2}}. Then x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub> are the roots of X<sup>2</sup> − {{b_e1}}X + {{b_e2}}, which are {{b_x1}} and {{b_x2}}, both in F<sub>{{b_p}}</sub> and both with points on the curve. Checking the four sign choices gives R = {{b_shown_expr}}, and so the relation

blocks.label: One equation in two unknowns, from one random multiple of P.

blocks.p: In general this step is a polynomial system: for n factor-base points it has n unknowns and degree 2n−1 in each, solved with Gröbner bases rather than one resultant. The summation polynomials page covers what that costs.

The code repeated this for random multiples of P until it had {{b_rows_minus_cols}} more relations than unknowns. It took {{b_attempts}} attempts to find {{b_relations}} relations, a success rate of {{b_sampled_frac}}%.

At this size the true rate can be computed outright, by adding every pair of the {{b_members}} factor-base points and counting the distinct results. Exactly {{b_decomposable}} of the {{b_nonzero}} nonzero points are sums of two factor-base points: {{b_exact_frac}}%. Counting pairs alone, {{b_pairs}} of them, would suggest {{b_pairs_frac}}%, but different pairs can give the same sum; treating the sums as random points gives 1 − e<sup>−{{b_pairs}}/{{b_nonzero}}</sup> = {{b_poisson_frac}}%, close to the exact figure. Gaudry's heuristic probability, 1/n! = 1/2, is the leading term of the same count. This run's {{b_sampled_frac}}% is within sampling error of the exact value.
Each relation involves at most two unknowns, so the matrix is extremely sparse:

Gaussian elimination modulo {{b_n}} gives the matrix rank {{b_rank}}, and determines {{b_determined}} of the {{b_cols}} logarithms uniquely; the build checks each by scalar multiplication. The other {{b_undetermined}} stay free even though there are more equations than unknowns. With two unknowns per equation, the relations form a graph on the factor base, and a logarithm is pinned down only when its part of the graph contains a suitable cycle; parts that are trees leave one degree of freedom each. Collecting more relations closes them. The descent below only needs two determined logarithms, so the code stops here.

sections.heading: What this does and does not show

blocks.p: It shows the pipeline: factor base, relations, sparse linear algebra, descent, and, on the elliptic side, the summation polynomial and the Weil restriction that turn point decomposition into polynomial solving over a smaller field.

It does not show a speedup. Pollard's rho on this group would expect about √(πn/2) ≈ {{b_rho_steps}} steps, each one point addition. Index calculus used {{b_attempts}} decomposition attempts, each costing a resultant and a root search, plus the linear algebra. For n = 2, Gaudry's complexity Õ(q<sup>2−2/n</sup>) = Õ(q) has the same exponent as rho's O(q<sup>n/2</sup>) = O(q), and the constants favour rho. The advantage starts at n = 3, where Õ(q<sup>4/3</sup>) beats q<sup>3/2</sup>, and grows with n, but so does the degree of the polynomial systems, which is where the real difficulty lives.

blocks.note: Everything in Part 2 depends on Fq2 having the subfield Fq to put the factor base in. A curve over a prime field has no subfield, and no one has found a replacement factor base that works. That is why P-256, secp256k1 and Curve25519 are unaffected by this family of attacks, as the ECDLP note explains, and why the three settings behave so differently.
